description: I'm Pranjal Saxena, a data science student and independent astrophysics researcher. Outside science, I'm also a writer and theatre performer. I want to explore challenging scientific problems through research, mathematics, programming, and creative thinking. I care about asking the right questions, questioning my own assumptions, and making sense of complicated ideas without oversimplifying them. For me, curiosity is where it all begins.
summary: Six Months Apart is a public web tool that shows how a spot of sky changes across NASA's SPHEREx observations. Pick one of NASA's five test targets and it plays the real SPHEREx images as a short video, with per-pass stacks, difference images, quality flags, Gaia star markers and a spectrum built on the fly. It checks wavelength, flags and noise before calling a change real, and says "cannot tell" when it cannot. It also lets anyone measure the distance to the dwarf planet Makemake with three clicks on real images: 52.7 au, against 52.73 au from NASA JPL Horizons.
details:
What it does. Six Months Apart plays every SPHEREx Level-2 image of a spot as a short video, one detector at a time. Users can blink single images, add the images of each survey pass, subtract one pass from another, overlay Gaia DR3 stars moved to each image’s date, show quality flags, and click any source for a spectrum across 0.75 to 5 µm. The address bar holds the view, so any view can be shared.

How it works. A Python server (FastAPI, Astropy) finds the images at the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive and reads only the needed pixels from the public AWS mirror. It subtracts the archive’s zodiacal-light model and resamples each image north-up. A React and TypeScript front end draws the images and does the photometry in the browser. The five NASA targets and the Makemake exercise are saved as static files, so they work without the server. Search at any coordinates is built and passed its test against the real archive on 14 November. It is not publicly hosted, because the archive’s query service was down during the submission weekend.

What we found in real data. Barnard’s Star moves visibly north between passes. WISE 0855-0714 is about 2 arcminutes from NASA’s 2010 coordinates and is blended with a background star. Its extra light beyond 4 µm, where an ordinary star fades, shows the brown dwarf. Barnard’s Star, RW Aurigae and R Draconis are saturated, so the tool reports that instead of a false change or spectrum.

Benefits. SPHEREx photographs each spot in a different colour every time, and the tool lets anyone tell a real change in the sky from that camera effect. Anyone can also measure something real: Makemake’s distance from parallax, 52.7 au against 52.73 au from NASA JPL Horizons.

Tools. Python, Astropy, FastAPI, NumPy, TypeScript, React, Vite, astronomy-engine, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages.
